data.name: Farm for your Life
data.detailed_description:
Your community was taken down by a heavy storm which caused an apocalypse and unleashed the living dead. Together with the other survivors, it is your task to rebuild and to allow that sustainable life can still be assured. Cultivate your farm and manage your restaurant to provide food and deal with all the zombies.

It’s a strange Time Management Game. The light-hearted style of a casual game collides with elements, which are usually only seen in horror genres. Discover the contrast, which takes both genres for a wild ride.

Key Features


  • Combining elements from farming, tower defense and time-management genres
  • Set up and cultivate your farm with a lot of different fruits, vegetables and animals
  • Build, manage and upgrade your own restaurant and provide the others with a wide variety of dishes
  • Protect your farm by building mazes and towers. Our zombies are vicious vegetarians!
  • Design your own character
  • Get stuck in an unbloody, fruity survival-feeling
  • Story mode provides 5-6hours of gameplay
  • Peaceful mode for dedicated farmers
  • Original soundtrack

reviews.review:
Farm for your Life takes several familiar casual-game ideas and combines them into a surprisingly distinctive post-apocalyptic management experience. Instead of presenting the zombie apocalypse as a grim struggle filled with weapons and gore, it asks you to rebuild a community through agriculture, cooking, restaurant management, and defensive planning. Developed and published by Hammer Labs, the game has a playful personality that makes its unusual mixture of farming simulation, time management, and tower defense feel more cohesive than the premise initially suggests.

The story begins after a powerful storm devastates the community and coincides with the arrival of the living dead. As one of the survivors, your responsibility is not simply to stay alive but to restore a sustainable way of living. Farming becomes the foundation of this recovery. You cultivate different fruits and vegetables, work with animals, gather ingredients, and steadily expand your ability to provide food. The agricultural mechanics are intentionally accessible rather than highly realistic, so planting and harvesting rarely become complicated. This makes the game particularly suitable for players who enjoy farming concepts but do not necessarily want the detailed economic systems of a hardcore simulator.

What gives the farming greater purpose is its connection to the restaurant. Produce is not merely grown for profit or stored indefinitely. Ingredients can be transformed into meals that are served to other survivors, introducing a time-management element into the gameplay loop. The restaurant can be improved as progress is made, and a broader selection of dishes gradually becomes available. Balancing crop production with customer demand creates some of the game's most entertaining moments because decisions made on the farm directly affect how effectively the restaurant operates.

Then there are the zombies, which provide the game's strangest twist. These undead enemies have an appetite for your crops, turning the farm itself into territory that must be protected. Defensive structures and maze-like layouts can be created to control their approach, bringing basic tower-defense strategy into the otherwise peaceful management formula. The system is not as elaborate as what would be found in a dedicated tower-defense game, but that simplicity works within the larger design. Defense becomes another responsibility to juggle rather than completely taking over the experience.

The contrast between peaceful farming and zombie survival is strengthened by the cheerful visual presentation. The game avoids graphic horror and instead adopts a colorful, cartoon-like style. Zombies feel more mischievous than terrifying, while the farm and restaurant maintain the relaxed atmosphere expected from a casual simulation. This approach gives the game considerable charm. It can explore an apocalyptic scenario without becoming stressful or disturbing, making it accessible even to players who would normally have little interest in zombie games.

Progression also benefits from the variety of activities. You can customize your character, improve the farm, develop the restaurant, experiment with different crops and dishes, and strengthen your defenses. The story mode is relatively compact at approximately five to six hours, so this is not intended to compete with enormous farming games capable of consuming hundreds of hours. The shorter campaign instead allows its different mechanics to appear regularly without requiring an excessive commitment.

Peaceful mode is particularly useful for anyone more interested in agriculture than fighting off the undead. Removing or reducing the pressure associated with survival allows the farming side of the experience to take center stage. This flexibility demonstrates one of the game's better qualities: it does not demand that every player enjoy all of its genre influences equally. Those attracted to management can concentrate on efficiency, while others can find enjoyment in designing defenses and dealing with zombie attacks.

Its biggest limitation is that none of the individual systems possess exceptional depth. Farming is enjoyable but relatively straightforward, restaurant management can become repetitive, and tower defense remains fairly lightweight. Players approaching it exclusively as a farming simulator, restaurant simulator, or strategy game may therefore find their preferred component underdeveloped. The better way to appreciate the game is as a collection of simple systems that constantly interact. Variety, rather than complexity, is its strongest quality.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently Unknown or Unverified, as there is no confirmed official Steam Deck compatibility rating available for the game. The Steam release does include Linux support alongside Windows and macOS, but that should not be interpreted as an official guarantee of flawless Steam Deck operation. Players intending to use a Deck should therefore expect that manual adjustments or compatibility considerations may be necessary.

Farm for your Life ultimately succeeds because it has a clear identity. Growing vegetables while operating a restaurant and constructing defenses against vegetarian zombies is an absurd combination, yet the mechanics complement one another surprisingly well. The modest campaign length and relatively shallow individual systems prevent it from becoming a definitive farming or management simulator, but its approachable design, humorous premise, peaceful alternative mode, and varied gameplay make it an enjoyable casual experience with plenty of personality.

Rating: 7/10
